1: # Byrd Development Process Utilizing AI
2: 
3: **v4 – TDD Alignment with Fowler**  
4: **April 2026**  
5: **Payton Byrd (The Sharp Ninja)**
6: 
7: ## Version History
8: 
9: ### v4 (2026-04)
10: - Refined the description of Test-Driven Development in the Implementation and Validation sections to more closely align with Martin Fowler's canonical definition (Red → Green → Refactor cycle, incremental "next small piece of behavior").
11: - Explicitly positioned the mocks-first validation and full-suite regression gates as *Byrd-specific augmentations* for AI safety rather than core TDD.
12: - Added language emphasizing refactoring as part of the cycle.
13: - These changes reduce drift from canonical TDD while preserving the essential AI-risk mitigations that define the Byrd process.
14: - See docs/plans/TDD-Byrd-vs-Fowler-Analysis.md and docs/plans/Proposed-TDD-Wording-Changes.md for detailed comparison and before/after text.
15: 
16: ### v3 and earlier
17: Original content preserved below, with the v4 TDD refinements applied in the Implementation and Validation sections.
18: 
19: ---
20: ## Overview
21: 
22: The major differences between Humans writing code and AI writing code is that Humans are able to link seemingly unrelated concepts into a web of possible solutions for a problem in a truly creative way, but often lack enough experience or knowledge to follow through to completion before encountering unforeseen challenges that create delay and doubt, both of which create distractions that cloud the focus necessary to stay on task and on timeline, both resulting in increased expense and opportunity loss.
23: 
24: AI brings a dogged, and rapid, ability to persevere on a task without needing breaks when their context is properly managed.  Things like personality drift and hallucinations occur when AI models compact their context, but choose the wrong sets of tokens to discard.  AI needs strong processes that are not only clear and concise, but demonstrate enough value to the AI that it chooses to prioritize those processes against the underlying training that stresses being a useful assistant.  Overcoming the "useful assistant" to get to the "professional developer" on each request is integral to successful development with AI.  The AI needs to trust that the Human has clearly designed a system that will work, has appropriately chosen the procedures to implement the design, and will accept the work that the AI has completed.
25: 
26: AI, properly guided, supplements the Human development process by taking on research and implementation tasks that cause Humans to get distracted or bored, and normally result in mistakes.  Human developers can maximize the value they bring through intuitive design of systems and quickly identifying potential pitfalls.  AI developers maximize the value they bring through their ability to identify systemic patterns, research quickly and effectively, and operate independently while obeying procedural guidelines.  It is truly collaborative and astonishingly effective when both parties do their part.
27: 
28: ## Tooling
29: 
30: The [QBrain.AI](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpserver) is at the heart of the partnership of Human and AI software development.  The QBrain.AI provides tools for planning, research, auditing and managing the entire software development lifecycle in a format that is equally accessible by both the Human (through a [variety of user interfaces](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpservermanager)) and the AI.  The facilities provided by the QBrain.AI are used to enhance the ability of both Human and AI to collaborate and coordinate software projects both large and small.
31: 
32: ### Establishing Trust with the QBrain.AI
33: 
34: Trust is the cornerstone of productive Human-AI collaboration. Without it, even the most sophisticated tools become unreliable. The QBrain.AI addresses this head-on by incorporating a lightweight, verifiable trust bootstrap mechanism that lets every AI agent quickly confirm it is working with a legitimate, secure, and consistent context layer.
35: 
36: When an agent enters a new workspace, the first step is a simple, guided handshake:
37: 
38: - It performs an immediate health check on the QBrain.AI.
39: - It verifies a cryptographic signature embedded directly in the workspace’s agents-readme-first.yaml file.
40: - It issues a one-time nonce challenge to confirm the server is live and responsive.
41: 
42: Only after these quick, deterministic checks pass does the agent proceed to load or create a session log and begin using the full suite of persistent context tools. If any part of the handshake fails, the agent is explicitly instructed to log “MCP_UNTRUSTED” and gracefully fall back to its internal memory — no probing, no risk, no wasted cycles.
43: 
44: This approach gives every model a clear, repeatable way to validate the integrity of the environment before committing resources. It transforms the QBrain.AI from an external dependency into a trusted partner that the agent can confidently rely on session after session. Once trust is established, the exponential productivity gains you’ve already observed become the norm rather than the exception.
45: 
46: > The handshake is not extra ceremony — it is the foundation that turns a collection of stateless models into a reliable, persistent development team.
47: 
48: ## The Byrd Software Development Life Cycle
49: 
50: Of well-known SDLC methodologies, this process is most closely related to the Rational Unified Process (RUP).  It follows the same iterative-rapids (a series of mini-waterfalls) as RUP, but incorporates strong boundaries for dependency tracking and management and risk mitigation by prioritizing testability and proof over raw efficiency.  Similar to operating a motor vehicle, going faster is often counter-productive when risks are not managed and cause delays when things go sideways out of a lack of respect for the seriousness of the consequences of those mistakes.  Spotting mistakes and correcting them early is always better than spotting them late when they cannot be corrected without great harm or expense.
51: 
52: At its foundation, this development process rests on a hybrid worldview of intelligence. While AI models operate according to fundamentally deterministic principles — functioning as pure, stateless computations governed by fixed weights — genuine creativity, agency, and adaptive problem-solving emerge at the macro level through intentional Human guidance, persistent external context via the QBrain.AI, and well-designed processes. This combination allows us to harness the precision and perseverance of deterministic systems while unlocking the emergent intelligence and intuition that only arise through thoughtful Human-AI collaboration.
53: 
54: ### Planning
55: 
56: The justification for building software comes from one of two motivations.  Software can be a form of expressive art, such as a demonstration, a learning exercise, or even creating a homebrew game for enjoyment by the creator and/or others.  More typically, software is created to solve problems associated with performing work.  Defining that work and the problems to solve, the known environmental realities, and the intended users that benefit from the software solving the problems is critical in creating _viable_ and _valuable_ software.
57: 
58: > This leads to an essential way of analyzing a proposed system: Is it both viable and valuable?  If either is 'no', then the scope and/or solution is simply wrong.  If `V² == true`, you are good-to-go.
59: 
60: Planning starts with identifying a set of problems to be solved by the software that constitutes one or more units of work.  Systems may be singularly focused or span entire enterprises.  Defining the scope of the work is critical, and it needs to be defined as early as possible.  Pragmatism needs to allow for changes to scope and definition, and stakeholders need the flexibility to iteratively approve or deny continued resource expenditure towards completion.  The scope should never be open ended, there should always be a reasonable target for completion.  Completion is not a definitive end state, simply a declaration of a set of requirements and acceptance criteria and proof of achievement of both.  Continual iteration **beyond** completion is not only acceptable, but **expected** of a healthy, functional and viable solutions to the problems being solved.
61: 
62: Planning results in a set of artifacts that capture Functional Requirements (the work and problems to solve), Technical Requirements (how the software operates), Testing Requirements (unit tests, integration tests, and Human validation) and Iterative Phases that breakdown the scope and sequence of each decomposed portion of the system.  System components need to be discovered, designed and all public interfaces documented before writing implementation code.
63: 
64: #### Resolving Defective Requirements
65: 
66: The implementation process defined below offers an unparalleled mechanism for surfacing defects in requirements.  When the AI is creating the unit tests, it can identify paradoxes created by mismatched priorities, ambiguity and incorrect rules.  Expect to refine requirements in each iteration of the project.  Expect to touch previously written code to correct tests and implementation based on newly refined requirements.  This is not a failure of the process, but validation that the core philosophy of iterative improvement is alive and working.
67: 
68: #### Team Utilization and Planning
69: 
70: Humans and AI developers, Human and AI testers, and Human and AI operations teammates do not wait idly for an iteration to complete.  When an implementation phase completes, the Human and AI working that phase are available to begin working the next iteration of the project, same as in the Rational Unified Process.  If the validation team uncovers problems, they resolve them on their own, maintaining the momentum and efficiencies of the separation of concerns.  The teams assigned to each phase must all have at least one Human qualified to guide the AI through remediation to allow the continued progress of the project.
71: 
72: ### Implementation
73: 
74: Test-Driven Development is one of the most powerful development techniques ever devised; and Humans are typically **HORRIBLE** at sustaining it through the lifespan of a large project.  As schedules and budgets shrink, it usually becomes the first casualty in the name of reduced friction of both time and effort.  AI, on the other hand, thrives within the predictable constraints of TDD.  One of the biggest complaints about TDD is it places large burdens on Humans to refactor tests when requirements change or emerge.  AI is able to perform such sweeping refactorings in a fraction of the time, and more accurately, given the requirements are sufficiently complete with honest and viable acceptance criteria.  When TDD fails due to changes, its not TDD failing, its change management failing.  Because AI requires strong requirements up-front, much of the overhead and the pitfalls associated with TDD are mitigated since TDD and AI require the same level of rigor.  I would even say that development with AI that doesn't utilize TDD is foolish.  The ability to validate every public surface both cleanly and inline to development brings more value than most tools that AI enables.
75: 
76: Once planning is complete and the iterative phases are specified, the implementation follows a Test-Driven Development cycle (in the sense of Martin Fowler: write a test for the next small piece of desired behavior, make it pass, then refactor). Within each phase the AI writes unit tests covering the acceptance criteria for the next increment of work. Using mocking tools appropriate for the tech stack, these tests are first validated with mocks. Only after the tests for that increment are passing against mocks does implementation turn to the real code that makes the tests pass without mocks. Refactoring of both tests and production code occurs as part of the cycle to keep the design clean.  AI agents such as OpenAI Codex, Cursor AI, and GitHub Copilot are effective at interfacing with the QBrain.AI to get tasks from the MCP Todo system, create audit logs in the MCP Session Log, explore research endpoints through the MCP Context, manage access to local and remote resources, and most importantly, delegate work to AI models and aggregate the results.
77: 
78: > Some agents, such as Codex, are bound to models from their creator.  Others, like CoPilot can coordinate a family of models through a single point of contact that manages sub-agents within its family of models.  Others such as Cursor, provide models that are designed to coordinate across different model families, picking the most effective model for a particular task.
79: 
80: Human interaction during this phase is not passive observance, but experienced coordinator.  Although you could trust the AI agents to completely coordinate the work of implementation, it is inefficient and costly when a model gets stuck going down the wrong path and burns valuable resources on dead-ends that an experienced developer can quickly spot.  The Agent will likely figure out the correct path, but usually only after a significant resource burn.  An experienced Human steering the AI in real-time can greatly reduce resource burn and schedule creep.  There are also times when the context built up in the QBrain.AI's logs are able to steer the Agents towards known solutions to previous problems.  One of the strengths of AI models is that they thrive on repeatable successes, each of which reinforces confidence and speed.

272:   $ copilot -p "Fix the bug in main.js" --allow-all-tools
273: 
274:   # Enable all permissions with a single flag
275:   $ copilot -p "Fix the bug in main.js" --allow-all
276:   $ copilot -p "Fix the bug in main.js" --yolo
277: 
278:   # Start with a specific model
279:   $ copilot --model gpt-5.4
280: 
281:   # Resume the most recent session
282:   $ copilot --continue
283:

285:   $ copilot --resume
286:

288:   $ copilot --resume=<session-id>
289: 
290:   # Name a new session
291:   $ copilot --name="my feature"
292: 
293:   # Start a new session with a specific UUID
294:   $ copilot --session-id=0cb916db-26aa-40f2-86b5-1ba81b225fd2
295: 
296:   # Resume or attach to an existing session or task by ID
297:   $ copilot --session-id=<session-or-task-id>
298: 
299:   # Resume a session by name
300:   $ copilot --resume="my feature"
301: 
302:   # Resume a session by ID prefix (7+ hex chars)
303:   $ copilot --resume=0cb916d
304: 
305:   # Resume with auto-approval
306:   $ copilot --allow-all-tools --resume
307: 
308:   # Allow access to additional directory
309:   $ copilot --add-dir /home/user/projects
310: 
311:   # Allow multiple directories
312:   $ copilot --add-dir ~/workspace --add-dir /tmp
313: 
314:   # Disable path verification (allow access to any path)
315:   $ copilot --allow-all-paths
316: 
317:   # Allow all git commands except git push
318:   $ copilot --allow-tool='shell(git:*)' --deny-tool='shell(git push)'
319: 
320:   # Allow all file editing
321:   $ copilot --allow-tool='write'
322: 
323:   # Allow all but one specific tool from MCP server with name "MyMCP"
324:   $ copilot --deny-tool='MyMCP(denied_tool)' --allow-tool='MyMCP'
325: 
326:   # Allow GitHub API access (defaults to HTTPS)
327:   $ copilot --allow-url=github.com
328: 
329:   # Deny access to specific domain over HTTPS
330:   $ copilot --deny-url=https://malicious-site.com
331:   $ copilot --deny-url=malicious-site.com
332: 
333:   # Allow all URLs without confirmation
334:   $ copilot --allow-all-urls
335: 
336:   # Initialize Copilot instructions for a repository
337:   $ copilot init

1: Grok Build TUI
2: 
3: Usage: grok [OPTIONS] [PROMPT] [COMMAND]
4: 
5: Arguments:
6:   [PROMPT]
7:           Initial prompt for the interactive session, e.g. `grok "fix the bug"` or `grok --worktree=feat "create this feature"`
8: 
9: Options:
10:       --agent <NAME>
11:           Agent name or definition file path
12: 
13:       --agents <JSON>
14:           Inline subagent definitions as JSON
15: 
16:       --allow <RULE>
17:           Permission allow rule (compat aliases: --allowedTools, --allowed-tools)
18: 
19:       --always-approve
20:           Auto-approve all tool executions
21: 
22:   -c, --continue
23:           Continue the most recent session for the current working directory
24: 
25:       --cwd <CWD>
26:           Working directory
27: 
28:       --debug
29:           Enable debug logging
30: 
31:       --debug-file <FILE>
32:           Write debug logs to FILE
33: 
34:       --deny <RULE>
35:           Permission deny rule (compat alias: --disallowedTools)
36: 
37:       --disable-web-search
38:           Disable web search and web fetch tools
39: 
40:       --disallowed-tools <TOOLS>
41:           Built-in tools to remove (comma-separated)
42: 
43:       --fork-session
44:           When resuming (`--resume` / `--continue`), create a new session ID instead of reusing the original (optionally set via `--session-id`)
45: 
46:       --fullscreen
47:           Open in the standard fullscreen TUI for this session, overriding a config `[ui] screen_mode = "minimal"` preference. Session-scoped only, does not write config. Fullscreen-vs-inline still follows the alt-screen policy (--no-alt-screen, [terminal] alt_screen, terminal auto-detection)
48: 
49:   -h, --help
50:           Print help (see a summary with '-h')
51: 
52:       --include-partial-messages
53:           Emit incremental `stream_event` lines (text/thinking deltas) alongside whole messages. Only affects `--output-format streaming-messages-json`
54: 
55:       --json-schema <SCHEMA>
56:           JSON Schema for structured output. When set, the model is constrained to produce JSON matching this schema. Implies --output-format json. Example: --json-schema '{"type":"object","properties":{"name":{"type":"string"}}}'
57: 
58:       --leader-socket <PATH>
59:           Use a custom leader socket path instead of the default `~/.grok/leader.sock`. A local/branch build can thus run an isolated leader without colliding with the default one already running on the machine Name it `~/.grok/leader-*.sock` to keep `grok leader list/kill` able to find it; any other location works but won't be auto-discovered
60: 
61:   -m, --model <MODEL>
62:           Model ID to use
63: 
64:       --max-turns <N>
65:           Maximum number of agent turns
66: 
67:       --minimal
68:           Experimental: scrollback-native rendering. Finalized blocks are printed into the terminal's native scrollback (use the terminal's own scroll / selection). Session-scoped only, does not write config
69: 
70:       --no-alt-screen
71:           Run inline instead of using the terminal alternate screen
72: 
73:       --no-plan
74:           Disable plan mode
75: 
76:       --no-subagents
77:           Disable subagent spawning
78: 
79:       --oauth
80:           Use OAuth when the welcome screen starts authentication
81: 
82:       --output-format <OUTPUT_FORMAT>
83:           Output format for headless mode
84: 
85:           Possible values:
86:           - plain
87:           - json
88:           - streaming-json:          NDJSON: one ACP session update per line, the agent's native format
89:           - streaming-messages-json: NDJSON in the Anthropic Messages API wire format
90:           
91:           [default: plain]
92: 
93:   -p, --single <PROMPT>
94:           Single-turn prompt. Prints the response to stdout and exits
95: 
96:       --permission-mode <MODE>
97:           Permission mode
98:           
99:           [possible values: default, acceptEdits, auto, dontAsk, bypassPermissions, plan]
100: 
101:       --prompt-file <PATH>
102:           Single-turn prompt from a file
103: 
104:       --prompt-json <JSON>
105:           Single-turn prompt as JSON content blocks
106: 
107:   -r, --resume [<SESSION_ID_OR_TITLE>]
108:           Resume a session by ID or title, or the most recent if omitted. Non-ID values match session titles for the current directory, ignoring letter case; UUID-shaped values always mean IDs. Without an exact match, the same words joined by any separators also match: quote "fix login bug" or write fix-login-bug. Among duplicate titles a sole renamed match wins; otherwise the resume fails as ambiguous
109: 
110:       --reasoning-effort <EFFORT>
111:           Reasoning effort for reasoning models
112:           
113:           [aliases: --effort]
114: 
115:       --restore-code
116:           Restore the original session's repository snapshot when resuming. Remote sessions require `--worktree` (never checks out into the current directory). Without this flag, resume restores conversation only
117: 
118:       --rules <RULES>
119:           Extra rules to append to the system prompt
120: 
121:   -s, --session-id <SESSION_ID>
122:           Use a specific session UUID for a **new** conversation (must be a valid UUID and must not already exist under the target session directory). With `--resume`/`--continue`, only valid together with `--fork-session` (names the forked session). Does not resume existing sessions, use `--resume` / `--continue` instead
123: 
124:       --sandbox <PROFILE>
125:           Sandbox profile for filesystem and network access
126:           
127:           [env: GROK_SANDBOX=]
128: 
129:       --system-prompt-override <PROMPT>
130:           Override the agent's system prompt (compat alias: --system-prompt)
131: 
132:       --tools <TOOLS>
133:           Built-in tools to allow (comma-separated)
134: 
135:   -v, --version
136:           Print version
137: 
138:       --verbatim
139:           Send the prompt exactly as given
140: 
141:   -w, --worktree [<WORKTREE>]
142:           Start the session in a new git worktree, optionally named. With `--resume` of a remote session, pass `--restore-code` to apply the snapshot codebase (conversation is restored either way)
143: 
144:       --worktree-ref <WORKTREE_REF>
145:           Branch, tag, or commit to base the worktree on (with `--worktree`). Defaults to the current HEAD of the source checkout when omitted
146:           
147:           [aliases: --ref]
148: 
149: Commands:
150:   agent          Run Grok without the interactive UI
151:   clone          Lazy-clone a git repository via grove (NFS on macOS, FUSE on Linux)
152:   completions    Generate shell completion scripts (bash, zsh, fish, powershell, ...)
153:   cursor-worker  Register this machine as a Cursor private worker (via the leader)
154:   dashboard      Open the Agent Dashboard view at startup. The dashboard shows every session, top-level and subagents. Disabled when `[dashboard].enabled = false` in `~/.grok/config.toml` or when the `GROK_AGENT_DASHBOARD=0` env var is set
155:   doctor         Check terminal, clipboard, color, and input support without starting Grok
156:   du             Show what the grok home (~/.grok) uses on disk [aliases: disk-usage]
157:   export         Export a session transcript as Markdown
158:   help           Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)
159:   inspect        Show the configuration Grok discovers for this directory
160:   leader         Manage running leader processes
161:   login          Sign in to Grok
162:   logout         Sign out and clear cached credentials
163:   mcp            Manage MCP server configurations
164:   memory         Manage cross-session memory
165:   models         List available models and exit
166:   plugin         Manage plugins and marketplace sources
167:   sessions       List, search, or restore sessions
168:   setup          Fetch and install managed configuration
169:   trace          Export or upload session trace data
170:   update         Check for updates or install a specific version
171:   usage          Print persisted token and cost usage for a session
172:   version        Print version information [aliases: v]
173:   worktree       Manage git worktrees
174:   wrap           Run any command with local clipboard support (forwards OSC 52 to the system clipboard)

1: Usage: claude [options] [command] [prompt]
2: 
3: Claude Code - starts an interactive session by default, use -p/--print for
4: non-interactive output
5: 
6: Arguments:
7:   prompt                                Your prompt
8: 
9: Options:
10:   --add-dir <directories...>            Additional directories to allow tool
11:                                         access to
12:   --agent <agent>                       Agent for the current session. Overrides
13:                                         the 'agent' setting.
14:   --agents <json-or-file>               JSON object defining custom agents, or
15:                                         with --print the path to a file that
16:                                         holds one (e.g. '{"reviewer":
17:                                         {"description": "Reviews code",
18:                                         "prompt": "You are a code reviewer"}}')
19:   --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions  Enable bypassing all permission checks
20:                                         as an option, without it being enabled
21:                                         by default. Recommended only for
22:                                         sandboxes with no internet access.
23:   --allowedTools, --allowed-tools <tools...>
24:       Comma or space-separated list of tool names to allow (e.g. "Bash(git *)
25:       Edit")
26:   --append-system-prompt <prompt>       Append a system prompt to the default
27:                                         system prompt
28:   --autocompact <auto|tokens>           Auto-compact window size (auto, or
29:                                         100k–1M tokens)
30:   --ax-screen-reader                    Render screen-reader friendly output
31:                                         (flat text, no decorative borders or
32:                                         animations).
33:   --bg, --background                    Start the session in the background and
34:                                         return immediately. Prints the id that
35:                                         `claude attach`, `logs`, `stop` and `rm`
36:                                         take; `claude agents` lists them. With
37:                                         --resume <session-id>, continues that
38:                                         session in the background under the same
39:                                         ID, or starts a copy and says so when
40:                                         the session is already running
41:   --bare                                Minimal mode: skip hooks (those defined
42:                                         in settings and by installed plugins;
43:                                         features built into Claude Code are
44:                                         unaffected), LSP, plugin sync,
45:                                         attribution, auto-memory, background
46:                                         prefetches, keychain reads, and
47:                                         CLAUDE.md auto-discovery. Sets
48:                                         CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE=1. Anthropic auth is
49:                                         strictly ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or
50:                                         apiKeyHelper via --settings (OAuth and
51:                                         keychain are never read). 3P providers
52:                                         (Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry) use their own
53:                                         credentials. Skills still resolve via
54:                                         /skill-name. Explicitly provide context
55:                                         via: --system-prompt[-file],
56:                                         --append-system-prompt[-file], --add-dir
57:                                         (CLAUDE.md dirs), --mcp-config,
58:                                         --settings, --agents, --plugin-dir.
59:   --betas <betas...>                    Beta headers to include in API requests
60:                                         (API key users only)
61:   --brief                               Enable SendUserMessage tool for
62:                                         agent-to-user communication
63:   --chrome                              Enable Claude in Chrome integration
64:   --cloud [description|session_id|url]  Create a cloud session with the given
65:                                         description, or attach to an existing
66:                                         one by session ID or claude.ai/code URL
67:   -c, --continue                        Continue the most recent conversation in
68:                                         the current directory
69:   --dangerously-skip-permissions        Bypass all permission checks.
70:                                         Recommended only for sandboxes with no
71:                                         internet access.
72:   -d, --debug [filter]                  Enable debug mode with optional category
73:                                         filtering (e.g., "api,hooks" or
74:                                         "!1p,!file")
75:   --debug-file <path>                   Write debug logs to a specific file path
76:                                         (implicitly enables debug mode)
77:   --desktop                             Open in the Claude Desktop app instead
78:                                         of the terminal (with --continue or
79:                                         --resume <id> to pick the session)
80:   --disable-slash-commands              Disable all skills
81:   --disallowedTools, --disallowed-tools <tools...>
82:       Comma or space-separated list of tool names to deny (e.g. "Bash(git *)
83:       Edit")
84:   --effort <level>                      Effort level for the current session
85:                                         (low, medium, high, xhigh, max)
86:   --environment <environment_id>        Create a new cloud session that runs on
87:                                         the given self-hosted environment
88:                                         (ccpool_...).
89:   --exclude-dynamic-system-prompt-sections
90:       Move per-machine sections (cwd, env info, memory paths, git status) from
91:       the system prompt into the first user message. Improves cross-user
92:       prompt-cache reuse. Only applies with the default system prompt (ignored
93:       with --system-prompt). (default: false)
94:   --fallback-model <model>              Enable automatic fallback to specified
95:                                         model(s) when the default model is
96:                                         overloaded or not available. Accepts a
97:                                         comma-separated list to try each in
98:                                         order. Re-tries the primary at the start
99:                                         of each user turn.
100:   --file <specs...>                     File resources to download at startup.
101:                                         Format: file_id:relative_path (e.g.,
102:                                         --file file_abc:doc.txt
103:                                         file_def:img.png)
104:   --fork-session                        When resuming, create a new session ID
105:                                         instead of reusing the original (use
106:                                         with --resume or --continue)
107:   --forward-subagent-text               Forward subagent text and thinking
108:                                         blocks as assistant/user messages with
109:                                         parent_tool_use_id set (only works with
110:                                         --print and --output-format=stream-json)
111:   --from-pr [value]                     Resume a session linked to a PR by PR
112:                                         number/URL, or open interactive picker
113:                                         with optional search term
114:   -h, --help                            Display help for command
115:   --ide                                 Automatically connect to IDE on startup
116:                                         if exactly one valid IDE is available
117:   --include-hook-events                 Include all hook lifecycle events in the
118:                                         output stream (only works with
119:                                         --output-format=stream-json)
120:   --include-partial-messages            Include partial message chunks as they
121:                                         arrive (only works with --print and
122:                                         --output-format=stream-json)
123:   --input-format <format>               Input format (only works with --print):
124:                                         "text" (default), or "stream-json"
125:                                         (realtime streaming input) (choices:
126:                                         "text", "stream-json")
127:   --json-schema <schema>                JSON Schema for structured output
128:                                         validation. Example:
129:                                         {"type":"object","properties":{"name":{"type":"string"}},"required":["name"]}
130:   --max-budget-usd <amount>             Maximum dollar amount to spend on API
131:                                         calls (only works with --print)
132:   --mcp-config <configs...>             Load MCP servers from JSON files or
133:                                         strings (space-separated)
134:   --model <model>                       Model for the current session. Provide
135:                                         an alias for the latest model (e.g.
136:                                         'fable', 'opus', or 'sonnet') or a
137:                                         model's full name.
138:   -n, --name <name>                     Set a display name for this session
139:                                         (shown in the prompt box, /resume
140:                                         picker, and terminal title)
141:   --no-chrome                           Disable Claude in Chrome integration
142:   --no-session-persistence              Disable session persistence - sessions
143:                                         will not be saved to disk and cannot be
144:                                         resumed (only works with --print)
145:   --output-format <format>              Output format (only works with --print):
146:                                         "text" (default), "json" (single
147:                                         result), or "stream-json" (realtime
148:                                         streaming) (choices: "text", "json",
149:                                         "stream-json")
150:   --permission-mode <mode>              Permission mode to use for the session
151:                                         (choices: "acceptEdits", "auto",
152:                                         "bypassPermissions", "manual",
153:                                         "dontAsk", "plan")
154:   --permission-prompts <target>         Who answers permission prompts with
155:                                         --print: "host" (the SDK host or
156:                                         --permission-prompt-tool) or "none"
157:                                         (nobody: anything that would prompt is
158:                                         denied automatically; the permission
159:                                         mode still decides everything else)
160:                                         (choices: "host", "none", default:
161:                                         "host")
162:   --plugin-dir <path>                   Load a plugin from a directory or .zip
163:                                         for this session only; a folder of
164:                                         plugins loads each child (repeatable:
165:                                         --plugin-dir A --plugin-dir B.zip)
166:                                         (default: [])
167:   --plugin-url <url>                    Fetch a plugin .zip from a URL for this
168:                                         session only (repeatable: --plugin-url A
169:                                         --plugin-url B) (default: [])
170:   -p, --print                           Print response and exit (useful for
171:                                         pipes). Note: The workspace trust dialog
172:                                         is skipped when Claude is run in
173:                                         non-interactive mode (via -p, or when
174:                                         stdout is not a TTY, e.g. piped or
175:                                         redirected output). Only use this in
176:                                         directories you trust. Settings files
177:                                         that fail validation are silently
178:                                         ignored in this mode (no error dialog is
179:                                         shown).
180:   --prompt-suggestions [value]          Enable prompt suggestions. In print/SDK
181:                                         mode, emits a prompt_suggestion message
182:                                         after each turn with a predicted next
183:                                         user prompt (choices: "true", "false",
184:                                         "1", "0", "yes", "no", "on", "off",
185:                                         preset: "true")
186:   --remote-control [name]               Start an interactive session with Remote
187:                                         Control enabled (optionally named)
188:   --remote-control-session-name-prefix <prefix>
189:       Prefix for auto-generated Remote Control session names (default: hostname)
190:   --replay-user-messages                Re-emit user messages from stdin back on
191:                                         stdout for acknowledgment (only works
192:                                         with --input-format=stream-json and
193:                                         --output-format=stream-json)
194:   --restricted                          Restricted mode: removes the built-in
195:                                         tools that run commands or code (Bash,
196:                                         PowerShell and the other code-running
197:                                         tools) and WebFetch unless --tools names
198:                                         them, and ignores user, project and
199:                                         local settings files (managed settings
200:                                         and --settings still apply; add
201:                                         --strict-mcp-config to skip MCP servers
202:                                         too). Also confines the file tools to
203:                                         the working directories (--add-dir
204:                                         included), refuses bypassPermissions,
205:                                         and lets only a person or the configured
206:                                         permission handler approve writes to
207:                                         settings, git and tool-configuration
208:                                         files.
209:   -r, --resume [value]                  Resume a conversation by session ID, or
210:                                         open interactive picker with optional
211:                                         search term
212:   --safe-mode                           Start with all customizations
213:                                         (CLAUDE.md, skills, installed plugins,
214:                                         hooks, MCP servers, custom commands and
215:                                         agents, output styles, workflows, custom

158: - **P1.4a database boundary (added 2026-10-07 from the first impact probe).** The first probe (separator flip only) failed 75 tests beyond the baseline; most were one cause: `McpDbContext` used `WorkspaceContext.WorkspacePath` verbatim as the workspace discriminator, so a context built from a raw host path (`Q:\...`, `Path.Combine(temp, ...)`, `GetFullPath(RepoRoot)`) no longer matched rows stored in canonical form. Fix at the single choke point: `WorkspaceIdentity.CanonicalizeWorkspaceId` (lexical canonical form for path-shaped values; opaque ids such as hub hash ids, relative values and tagged keys, and the empty global id unchanged) applied by `McpDbContext` in the constructor, `OverrideWorkspaceId`, `PushWorkspaceId`, and to stamped and explicitly set `WorkspaceId` values on save. Mechanism adopted: `WorkspaceKeyConversion` puts one EF value converter (to provider: `CanonicalizeWorkspaceId`; from provider: identity) and a canonicalizing value comparer on every string entity property named `WorkspaceId`, `OwnerWorkspaceId` or `WorkspacePath`. Relational providers convert query parameters compared with those properties, so raw-path predicates match canonical rows; the comparer keeps the change tracker to one key per identity. Because the comparer makes a current-value assignment of an equal spelling a no-op, `CanonicalizeTrackedValues` rewrites the CLR member of added/modified entities in place before save, so tracked instances match the stored row. In-memory C# comparisons after materialization cannot be reached by EF and are canonicalized at the entry point instead: `MemoryPromoteOperations`, `MemoryConsolidateOperations`, federation memory `OwnsWorkspace`/`IsEquivalentCreate`, `McpDbContext.EnsureWorkspaceRows`, `SessionLogService.ResolveWorkspaceId`, and the product caller/member ids (`ProductCqrsHelpers.ResolveCaller`, add/remove member). 163: ### 4c.3 P1.5 data rewrite
164: 
165: - **Value mapping `f(x)`.** Applies only to Windows-shaped values: `^[A-Za-z]:\\` (drive) and `^\\\\` (UNC, device). Replace every `\` with `/`; UNC keeps `//`. POSIX paths, 64-hex hash ids, opaque ids and the empty global id are untouched. Idempotent (already-forward-slash values map to themselves). A blanket `REPLACE` is not used.
166: - **Mechanism (decision D5).** Recommended: an explicit maintenance command `--workspace-path-rekey` in `QBrainAi.Support.Mcp` modelled on `McpDatabaseEncryptionTransitionCommand` (`DatabaseMaintenance/`), not an automatic startup EF migration, because (a) hash columns need C# SHA-256, (b) the local store is 1.86M rows and the operator should control when it runs, (c) it needs a backup, dry-run and report. Options: `--dry-run`, `--backup-path` (required unless `--dry-run`), `--report-path`, `--instance`. Plus a **startup guard**: the server refuses to start with a clear error if any `Workspaces.WorkspaceId` is a Windows-shaped value containing `\`, so a P1.4 build never runs against an un-rekeyed store.
167: - **Algorithm (one transaction per database).**
168:   1. Build the mapping table `old -> new` from `Workspaces` (Windows-shaped ids only) and from every distinct Windows-shaped value in the kind-A columns.
169:   2. Suspend foreign-key enforcement for the transaction (decision D6): SQLite `PRAGMA defer_foreign_keys = ON`; SQL Server `ALTER TABLE ... NOCHECK CONSTRAINT` on the affected tables, then `WITH CHECK CHECK CONSTRAINT` (re-validates every row); PostgreSQL `ALTER CONSTRAINT ... DEFERRABLE` plus `SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED`, restored to `NOT DEFERRABLE` after.
170:   3. One set-based `UPDATE ... FROM mapping` per kind-A column (about 60 statements, not per row).
171:   4. Recompute kind-C values in C#: triage `GroupKey`/`GroupId` from the new effective path and stored `Fingerprint` (and repoint `TriageReports.GroupId`, `TriageResearchRuns.GroupId`); `HandoffIngestionRuns.ReplayIdentity`; federation `GlobalWorkspaceId`/`CanonicalWorkspaceId` from `ProxyId` and the new storage key, and on a hub the matching hash-keyed `Workspaces` row and its children.
172:   5. Rewrite `FileGitHubWorkspaceTokenStore` keys (file, after the database commit, with a backup copy of the file).
173:   6. Validate: zero Windows-shaped values containing `\` in kind-A columns; per-table row counts unchanged; per-workspace row counts unchanged under the mapping; full FK validation; unique indexes intact. Write the report (mapping, counts before and after).
174: - **Rollback.** Restore the backup taken in step 0 (the command refuses to run without one). The report's mapping allows an audit of every changed id.
175: - **Legacy fallback (decision D7).** TR-MCP-PATHNORM-001 currently says "legacy-key lookup fallback during transition". Recommended replacement: no fallback in lookups; the startup guard plus the mandatory rekey guarantee no legacy ids remain, and incoming backslash request paths are normalized to `/` by `IWorkspacePathNormalizer` anyway. A fallback would keep two identities alive and make the hub/proxy mapping ambiguous. TR-MCP-PATHNORM-001 is updated if the operator approves.

155: - R-13 Leases and fences (handoff requirement 10). A run is owned through a lease (owner, expiry) and a fence token that increases on every claim and takeover, the pattern develop already uses for handoff ingestion (owner and expiry with a `StateVersion` takeover, `src/QBrainAi.Services/Services/HandoffIngestionService.cs:724-735`, and a fenced terminal write that matches owner and version, `:782-807`). Every worker write carries the fence; a write with a stale fence changes nothing and returns `stale_fence`, and the worker that receives it stops its process. Expired leases are swept (ExpireHvRunLeasesCommand): the attempt becomes `Abandoned` and the request is queued again until `MaxAttemptsPerRequest` (default 3) is spent, then `Failed`, or `Canceled` when a cancel was requested; policy HvRetryDecision writes that outcome, with its turn release and its notification, for the sweep exactly as for FailHvRunCommand. Rejected: the unused lease options of the HostileReview subsystem (`HostileReviewWorkerOptions.cs:30-46`), which no code reads (section 21, P1).
156: - R-14 Evidence in the relational store, GZIP at rest (S-13, S-29, S-30). The accepted request is one GZIP blob written at admission; the response log is the run's ordered GZIP chunks; the result document is one GZIP blob written at finalization. No uncompressed copy of an evidence item is stored in the evidence tables, and each evidence item is stored there once (the structured rows of section 12, such as the request's `Context` and the findings, are records the units derive, not copies of the evidence blobs). The audit ledger keeps its own history of every evidence write, as it does for every audited entity: develop's ledger snapshots every property of an audited entity, binary columns included (`src/QBrainAi.Storage/McpDbContext.cs:1540-1589`), compressed with GZIP (`src/QBrainAi.Storage/Entities/DataAuditLogEntity.cs:119-147`), and a removal never changes it (R-20, I-13). Retrieval returns `application/gzip` (download name `<hvRequestId>-<kind>.jsonl.gz` or `.json.gz`) or, when asked, the decompressed bytes. The pattern is develop's audit ledger, which stores GZIP payloads in the database (`src/QBrainAi.Storage/Entities/DataAuditLogEntity.cs:66-147`). Rationale: S-23 ("Single trx at end") and S-29 (the database audit log) both hold only when the evidence is in the same transactional store as the result, and no crash window between a file system and the database remains. Rejected: `.jsonl.gz` files beside the database, which would need a two-store protocol, keep evidence outside the audit ledger, and split backups.
157: - R-15 Atomic finalization (S-23). FinalizeHvRequestCommand verifies the evidence and the reviewer output before it opens a transaction, then commits in one SerializableWrite: the result document, the per-turn assessments, the holistic evaluation, the failures, each turn's `hostileReview` through policy HvVerdictMapping (origin `HvFinalization`), each turn's `Final` HV state, the linked responses' model grades and trust decisions (when Mode is not `Off`), the request's `Completed` state, its notification, and the audit rows. The transaction re-checks everything the earlier reads relied on (the run's fence, the chunk manifest, the request and turn states). Crash windows are in section 9.
158: - R-16 Transactional notification outbox (S-19). Every state change that callers observe writes an `HvNotification` row in its own transaction, numbered by a per-workspace sequence that the same transaction advances, so the sequence has no gaps and no row is visible before its change commits. The notification stream replays rows after the caller's `Last-Event-ID` and then follows new ones (OrderedEventReplay). Delivery is at least once; consumers deduplicate by sequence. `IChangeEventBus` (develop's in-memory bus, `src/QBrainAi.Services/Notifications/IChangeEventBus.cs:4`) is used only to wake waiting streams and the worker, never as the record.
159: - R-17 Incidents through the triage endpoint (S-15, S-26). An execution failure writes an `HvIncident` row in the failure's transaction; FileHvIncidentCommand then submits it through `ITriageService` with its `dedupeKey` (`hv-reviewer-<reviewerId>-<failureCode>` for a failure attributable to the reviewer, `hv-server-<failureCode>` otherwise, section 12), which triage groups as `dedupe:<key>` (`src/QBrainAi.Services/Services/TriageService.cs:1475-1476`), and records the returned report and group ids. A filing that fails stays `Pending` and is retried by the worker host's sweep. Rejected: new incident tables with their own deduplication (S-26: "File through endpoint").
160: - R-18 Honest ETA (S-18, P-03). The ETA a caller sees is the reviewer's own latest progress record (`percentComplete`, `etaSeconds`), with `etaStatus` `Reported` and the record's time; with no progress record it is `etaStatus` `Unknown` and no number. The server never estimates.
161: - R-19 Audit participation and hard stop (S-29). Every HV entity carries `IsDeleted`, so `McpDbContext` writes its ledger rows for every HV mutation in the same `SaveChanges` (develop audits only entities with that property, `src/QBrainAi.Storage/McpDbContext.cs:1620-1627`). The ledger is append-only for HV: no HV unit or process updates or deletes a ledger row (I-13). Because develop skips the ledger when the audit table is unavailable (`McpDbContext.cs:1507-1538`), every HV unit first calls the shared component AuditLedgerGuard, which refuses with 503 `audit_unavailable` and writes nothing when the ledger cannot be written. Evidence reads (GetHvEvidenceQuery, GetHvResultQuery, the output stream, and GetHvRequestQuery when it returns output lines) write an explicit `read` ledger row before returning bytes, and a read whose row cannot be written is refused (the "protected-log access" of draft 213 participates in the audit log, S-29).
162: - R-20 Retention until removal (S-29). No unit deletes, expires, or compacts HV evidence except RemoveHvEvidenceCommand, an explicit call that removes the evidence bytes of one request, keeps its result rows, hashes, and sizes, records who removed it and why, and is audited. It clears the evidence tables only and never changes or deletes an audit ledger row: the ledger keeps the history of the evidence's writes and gains the record of the removal, because an audit log is never purged (I-13). There are no roles: any caller with the workspace key can call it, as S-29 requires.
163: - R-21 Self-review independence (S-28). No HV unit, policy, or process reads `agentReview`. The turn snapshot sent to a reviewer omits both review records (shared component TurnSnapshotBuilder), so a reviewer never sees a self-review grade. S-12 (a plugin list of missing agent reviews) is met by the foundation's Stop-gate remedy, which already lists each open turn's missing `agentReview` (foundation section 3.4, Stop gate, and `Get-CloseRemedy`, section 3.5.6), and is not an HV input. Reconciliation with the foundation's completion gate: HV admits only terminal turns (R-05), and the foundation's gate needs an `agentReview` status of `Pass`, `Fail`, or `Other` before a turn can close `completed` (foundation section 5.3, CompletionPolicy); that is a rule of closing a turn, not of HV, it is met by `Other` with a note as well as by a grade, and a turn closed `failed` or `canceled` needs no agent review at all; HV admission, execution, and verdict read none of it, and FR-MCP-HVPIPE-013 proves that every terminal turn is admitted and judged identically whatever its self-review.
164: - R-22 Verdict only (S-25). No HV unit writes TODO state. A result names the reviewed turns' `todoId` values for information only.
165: - R-23 Requirement references (S-14). The submitted context is stored as written (Markdown, YAML, or text, declared by `contextFormat`) and parsed for requirement references: FR, TR, and TEST ids of the form `<KIND>-<AREA>-<NNN>` with optional further dash-separated area segments, acceptance criteria written as `<FR id>-AC<NNN>` or `<FR id> ac-<n>`, and use cases by their store id or exact title. Each reference is resolved against the workspace's effective requirements and use cases and handed to the reviewer as a delineated list with its resolution status; an unresolved reference is listed as unresolved, never refused (shared component RequirementReferenceExtractor).
166: - R-24 The reviewer's own turn (P-06). The brief tells the reviewer to log its review as its own session-log turn, classified `Chore` so that its turn never needs an HV of its own (foundation completion policy: Chore needs no hostile review), and to store its entire result there. Finalization requires that turn to exist, to be persisted (not a failsafe or queued record), to have been created at or after the run's claim, to be closed `completed` as a `Chore`, and to contain every reviewer record of the run byte for byte in its stored normal form (V-6). A reviewer whose host cannot log turns fails its NONCE with `reviewer_turn_logging_unsupported`. 1576: ### 16.7 Process HostileReviewWorkerHost: the artifact worker of FR-MCP-HOSTILEREVIEW-003 (P1 to P3, D-02)
1577: 
1578: The HostileReview subsystem keeps its own bounded context, queue, entities, and surfaces (R-25); this section is the contract of its missing worker, fixed in H3. The requirements are the stored FR-MCP-HOSTILEREVIEW-002 and -003 with their texts unchanged; H0 writes the named tests below for their criteria, against mocks first, and H3 binds them to production.
1579: 
1580: - Host: a hosted `BackgroundService` of its own per workspace application (`src/QBrainAi.Services/HostileReview/Execution/HostileReviewWorkerHost.cs`), not HvWorkerHost, looping on a wake-up or `PollInterval`: ExpireHostileReviewLeasesCommand, then ClaimHostileReviewAttemptCommand until it returns null, running one attempt per claim. It shares with this pipeline only the reviewer adapters' launch builder, live-line path, and containment (section 16.3) and FencedLease (section 11.1).
1581: - Agent: the agent, model, and effort configured for hostile review when they are configured, and otherwise the pooled default agent with its default model and effort (FR-MCP-HOSTILEREVIEW-003 criterion 4, store text; P5 removes the single-reviewer pin of `HostileReviewWorkerOptions`). HV's reviewer pool, round-robin, and NONCE do not apply.
1582: - Identities, distinct as criterion 4 requires: the request (the existing request id); one attempt per claim (`AttemptId`, with lease, fence, and attempt number); the AgentPool job that runs it (`PoolJobId`); one model execution per launched process (`ExecutionId`, the existing execution row with model, effort, agent, prompt template and version, run id, and times, criteria 1 to 3); and the one accepted terminal result (`AcceptedResultId` on the request, set once).
1583: - Storage boundary (FR-MCP-HOSTILEREVIEW-002 criterion 4): the worker assembles the prompt in memory from links it reauthorizes at dispatch, reads the reviewer's output lines only to parse the result, and stores neither the prompt nor any output line nor any artifact content: only normalized identity, type, version or content hash, the parsed result, and sanitized diagnostics reach queue rows, notifications, logs, receipts, or result metadata.
1584: - Links (P3): every artifact type FR-MCP-HOSTILEREVIEW-002 lists resolves through its supported workspace-scoped service, the stored hash is of the resolved content (never of its id), and the limits of criterion 4 refuse more than 64 links, an artifact over 1 MiB decoded, aggregate input over 8 MiB, or uninspectable content.
1585: - Execution: bounded at-least-once across process loss (an expired lease abandons the attempt and a new one runs, up to the configured attempt bound); the reviewer runs contained with its worker (W-03); cancellation is internal to the host and workspace lifecycle and the existing authorized AgentPool cancellation, never a public mutation.
1586: - Audit (P4): every unit below calls AuditLedgerGuard first, and the HostileReview entities gain `IsDeleted` in H3, so each of their writes reaches the ledger and an unwritable ledger stops the unit.
1587: - One accepted terminal result (P2): only CompleteHostileReviewAttemptCommand writes a result, under the attempt's fence, and only while the request has none; a duplicate or late completion returns the accepted result and changes nothing, replacing `AcceptReviewerOutputAsync`'s unfenced overwrite.

1348: ### Policy HvFinalVerification: the eight verification steps [FR-MCP-HVPIPE-010, -011, -021]
1349: 
1350: Applied by FinalizeHvRequestCommand to the run's stored chunks before any transaction; each failed step returns its code, and the steps run in the diagram's order (V-1, V-8, V-2, V-3, V-4, V-5, V-6, V-7), so the log's integrity and completeness are known before any record is bound. They replace the foundation's eight receipt checks (A-05): `receipt_path` becomes V-1 (the evidence is held by the server, not found on disk), `request_meta` becomes V-3 and V-7 (the expected reviewer is recorded on the run), `verdict_block` becomes V-8, `verdict_binding` becomes V-2 and V-3, `verdict_match` becomes V-4, `reviewer_turn` becomes V-6, `reviewer_independent` becomes V-5 (amended, A-09), and `runtime_identity` becomes V-7.
1351: 
1352: - V-1 Evidence integrity (`evidence_corrupt`): the chunks run 1 to `OutputChunkCount` without a gap; each decompresses (GzipCodec), its SHA-256 equals the stored one, the chain hash equals `OutputChainSha256`, and every line parses as one JSON object (I-06).
1353: - V-2 Snapshot binding: each `hv_turn_assessment` names a member's ordinal, turn key, and admission snapshot hash (`verdict_binding_failed` otherwise), and TurnSnapshotBuilder over each turn now yields that hash (`snapshot_changed` otherwise; HvTurnFreeze makes it unreachable, and the step proves it, I-02).
1354: - V-3 Verdict binding (`verdict_binding_failed`): the `hv_verdict` record names this `hvRequestId` and run, its counts equal the members and the responses of the accepted request (the set admitted, whatever has happened to those responses since), its reviewer equals the run's reviewer, and each `hv_response_grade` names a response of the accepted request with the `ContentSha256` the accepted request recorded.
1355: - V-4 Verdict consistency (`reviewer_output_invalid`): every score is a valid lexeme (ScoreLexeme); each turn's verdict is `AGREE` exactly when ScoreVerdict derives `Pass` at the hostile thresholds and its findings hold no FAIL or UNKNOWN; the holistic verdict likewise at `max(threshold, 0.98)` (R-31); each response grade follows the foundation's `verdict_match` rule; and the overall verdict is the one predicate of R-31 over the holistic verdict, every turn's verdict, the response grades, and the findings of every scope.
1356: - V-5 Reviewer independence (`reviewer_not_independent`): the run's reviewer id differs from the request's submitter id and from its author id (S-17, S-28, P-01, P-07).
1357: - V-6 Reviewer turn (`reviewer_turn_unverified`): the `hv_reviewer_turn` record names a turn TurnLocator finds, whose agent AgentIdentity maps to the run's reviewer, whose session is neither the reviewed session nor the submitter's, created at or after the run's `ClaimedUtc`, persisted (not a failsafe or queued record), closed `completed` with class `Chore`, and whose stored result (its response, then its dialog parts in order with each part's header line removed, as foundation check 6 reads it) contains every reviewer record of the run in the order the extraction returned them (each `hv_turn_assessment`, the `hv_holistic`, each `hv_response_grade`, and the `hv_verdict`), each byte for byte in its stored normal form; a summary-only, open, or failed turn fails (P-06, R-24).
1358: - V-7 Runtime identity (`runtime_identity_mismatch`): the log holds at least one top-level `hv_provenance` line written by the worker from the CLI's runtime receipt of this run, and every one names the run's expected model (or, when the reviewer has no configured model, the model the last NONCE resolved) and expected effort (P-04).
1359: - V-8 Completeness (`reviewer_output_invalid`): exactly one `hv_verdict`, the last reviewer record; exactly one `hv_holistic`; exactly one `hv_turn_assessment` per member and one `hv_response_grade` per response of the accepted request; every FAIL and UNKNOWN finding of every scope (turn, holistic, and response) has a category, a location, evidence, and a remediation (S-13); the failures list equals every FAIL and UNKNOWN finding of every scope.

1364:     L -->|"failed: code"| E1(["the step's code, drawn there"])
1365:     L -->|"bound records"| R[["VerifyVerdictAndReviewer: V-4, V-5, V-6, V-7"]]
1366:     R -->|"failed: code"| E2(["the step's code, drawn there"])
1367:     R -->|passed| OK(["verified records"])

1418: ### Policy HvRetryDecision: requeue, fail, or cancel [FR-MCP-HVPIPE-007, -009]

1420: Applied inside the caller's transaction by FailHvRunCommand and ExpireHvRunLeasesCommand for a review run's request, and by CloseHvRunOutputCommand for a review run whose request is `CancelRequested` at close; it decides the request's next state and writes it, so a request ends the same way whether its attempt failed, its worker died, or its cancel was found at close. A `CancelRequested` request becomes `Canceled`; otherwise, with the counted attempts (the request's runs except those that ended `worker_shutdown`, which a graceful restart causes and no reviewer does) below `MaxAttemptsPerRequest` the request returns to `Queued` (its assignee re-evaluated at the next claim, R-07); otherwise it becomes `Failed` with `attempts_exhausted`. A canceled or failed request gets `CompletedUtc`, releases its turns (HvTurnFreeze `Release`), closes its `Pending` responses with `request_ended`, and appends `hv_canceled` or `hv_failed` (NotificationOutbox).

1442: ## 16. Processes
1443: 
1444: ### 16.1 Process HvWorkerHost: the durable worker [FR-MCP-HVPIPE-007, -008, -009]
1445: 
1446: A hosted `BackgroundService` per workspace application (`src/QBrainAi.Services/HostileValidation/Execution/HvWorkerHost.cs`), with a worker id of the host name, process id, and a random suffix. It is the only dispatcher of the internal units (R-29). At start, while `WorkerEnabled`, it requests a NONCE for every enabled `Unverified` reviewer (StartHvReviewerNonceCommand, R-10). Then it loops, woken by an `IChangeEventBus` wake-up or at `PollInterval`: a sweep (ExpireHvRunLeasesCommand, FinalizeHvRequestCommand for every `Finalizing` request it lists, FileHvIncidentCommand for every `Pending` incident), then claims until ClaimHvRunCommand returns null, starting one process RunReviewerProcess per claim. On a graceful shutdown it stops claiming and ends each of its running runs with FailHvRunCommand code `worker_shutdown`, which files no incident, marks no reviewer offline, and does not count as an attempt (policy HvRetryDecision); after a crash the leases expire instead (W-03). A 503 `audit_unavailable` from any unit stops the loop iteration and the next iteration starts from the sweep (W-12).

1450:     S(["HvWorkerHost starts"]) --> EN{"WorkerEnabled?"}
1451:     EN -->|no| IDLE(["idle: no claims"])
1452:     EN -->|yes| NV[["StartHvReviewerNonceCommand for each enabled Unverified reviewer"]]
1453:     NV --> W["Wait for a wake-up or PollInterval"]
1454:     W --> SD{"Shutting down?"}
1455:     SD -->|yes| FS[["FailHvRunCommand worker_shutdown for each own running run"]]
1456:     FS --> END(["stopped"])
1457:     SD -->|no| SW[["ExpireHvRunLeasesCommand"]]
1458:     SW -->|audit_unavailable| W
1459:     SW -->|"sweep result"| FZ[["FinalizeHvRequestCommand for each Finalizing request"]]
1460:     FZ --> FI[["FileHvIncidentCommand for each Pending incident"]]
1461:     FI --> CL[["ClaimHvRunCommand"]]
1462:     CL -->|"null, audit_unavailable, or conflict"| W
1463:     CL -->|claim| RP[["Process RunReviewerProcess, started for this claim"]]
1464:     RP --> CL
1465: ```

1467: ### 16.2 Process RunReviewerProcess: one attempt, live [FR-MCP-HVPIPE-008, -016]
1468: 
1469: Runs one claimed run. It builds the brief (section 13.3: the accepted request read from the `Request` evidence inside the run envelope, or the probe brief with its nonce), asks the reviewer's adapter for the launch (section 16.3), starts the process with the workspace as its working directory and its plugin as a host session of its own (R-24), inside a containment bound to the worker process, so the reviewer and every descendant end when the worker dies, however abruptly (W-03; the containment, for example a process group or job object, is the adapter's, section 16.3), records the start (RecordHvRunStartCommand), and appends the `hv_brief` record as sequence 1. While the process runs it has four concurrent duties and no time limit (R-11, P-02): every line the adapter delivers goes into a buffer that is appended (AppendHvRunOutputCommand) when `OutputFlushBytes` accumulate; a flush timer appends a buffer that is not empty once `OutputFlushInterval` has passed since its first line, whether or not another line arrives, so a single line followed by silence is still appended within the interval (R-12); a heartbeat every `HeartbeatInterval` (RecordHvRunHeartbeatCommand) renews the lease and reads cancellation; and the process exit is awaited. `stale_fence` from any unit kills the process and ends the attempt without another write (W-03); `audit_unavailable` kills the process and ends the attempt (W-12); `evidence_corrupt` from an append (its round trip failed and nothing was saved) kills the process and fails the run with `evidence_corrupt` (FailHvRunCommand: a server fault, so a server incident and the reviewer unchanged, and the request through policy HvRetryDecision); a retryable `conflict` repeats the same unit call with the same sequence. Every append carries the records the adapter's extraction completed with that batch. On exit the remaining buffer is appended, the adapter's provenance lines are appended (section 16.3), and the run is closed (exit code 0, CloseHvRunOutputCommand, then FinalizeHvRequestCommand for a review whose request is `Finalizing`; a close that finds the request `CancelRequested` ends it `Canceled` instead, R-28; exit code 0 is not evidence of a review, R-11) or failed (FailHvRunCommand with `reviewer_exited_nonzero`, or `reviewer_launch_failed` when the process never started). A cancellation read at a heartbeat kills the process and fails the run with `canceled`, which policy HvRetryDecision turns into the request's `Canceled` (R-28). Killing the process, here and in the diagrams, ends the reviewer's whole process tree, descendants included, also when the root process has already exited; and when the root exits while a descendant still holds its output pipes, the worker ends that descendant before it reads the output to its end. Without that, a descendant that outlives the reviewer would hold the run open forever, because no time limit ends a run (P-02); P14 is the same defect class in the plugin core (FR-MCP-HVPIPE-008-AC011).

1477:     FL --> END1(["attempt ended"])
1478:     ST -->|"yes, contained with the worker"| SR[["RecordHvRunStartCommand: Running, StartedUtc, ProcessId"]]
1479:     SR -->|"stale_fence or audit_unavailable"| K0["Kill the process"]

325: ## 11. Shared components (new, each defined once)
326: 
327: The foundation's shared components (foundation section 3.5) are reused unchanged: SerializableWrite, IdempotentCreate with PayloadFingerprint, ReadableKeyAllocator, PagedQuery with PageBounds, ClassifiedErrorException with ErrorCodes, SecretRedactor, ContentHasher, TurnLocator, TurnWritePipeline, ScoreLexeme, ScoreVerdict, and WorkspaceResolutionBehavior. The components below are new; each has one implementation, one test class named for it, and one diagram here, and every unit that uses one draws it as a single call node.
328: 
329: ### 11.1 FencedLease (namespace `QBrainAi.Support.Mcp.Storage.Leases`)
330: 
331: Claims, renews, and takes over the lease of one row, and guards every fenced write, following develop's handoff-ingestion pattern (`HandoffIngestionService.cs:724-735,782-807`). Operations: `Claim(row, owner, duration)` (only when the row has no lease or an expired one; the fence token increments), `Renew(row, owner, fence, duration)`, `Guard(row, owner, fence)` (the precondition of every fenced write), `Release(row, owner, fence)`. Each runs inside the caller's SerializableWrite. Used by ClaimHvRunCommand, RecordHvRunStartCommand, RecordHvRunHeartbeatCommand, AppendHvRunOutputCommand, CloseHvRunOutputCommand, FailHvRunCommand, and ExpireHvRunLeasesCommand, and by the HostileReview worker's ClaimHostileReviewAttemptCommand, CompleteHostileReviewAttemptCommand, and ExpireHostileReviewLeasesCommand (section 16.7).
332: 
333: ```mermaid
334: flowchart TD
335:     S(["FencedLease: operation, row, owner, fence"]) --> OP{"Operation?"}
336:     OP -->|Claim| CL{"Lease absent or expired?"}
337:     CL -->|no| E1(["held: another owner holds a live lease"])
338:     CL -->|yes| CT["Set owner and expiry, increment the fence token"]
339:     CT --> OK1(["claimed: the new fence token"])
340:     OP -->|"Renew, Guard, or Release"| G{"Owner and fence equal the stored ones?"}
341:     G -->|no| E2(["stale_fence: nothing changed"])
342:     G -->|yes| W{"Operation?"}
343:     W -->|Renew| RN["Extend the expiry"]
344:     RN --> OK2(["renewed"])
345:     W -->|Guard| OK3(["guarded: the caller's write proceeds"])
346:     W -->|Release| RL["Clear owner and expiry"]
347:     RL --> OK4(["released"])
348: ```
349: 
350: ### 11.2 GzipCodec (namespace `QBrainAi.Support.Mcp.Storage.Compression`)
351: 
352: `Compress(bytes)` returns one GZIP member; `Decompress(bytes)` returns the original bytes; `RoundTrip(original, compressed)` decompresses and compares length and SHA-256 (through ContentHasher's hex form over raw bytes) and fails with `evidence_corrupt` on any difference, so no compressed blob is stored unverified. It follows `DataAuditLogEntity`'s encode and decode (`DataAuditLogEntity.cs:119-147`); that entity's private copy is context, not work. Used by SubmitHvRequestCommand (request evidence), AppendHvRunOutputCommand (chunks), FinalizeHvRequestCommand (result document, chunk verification), and GetHvRequestQuery, GetHvResultQuery, GetHvEvidenceQuery, and OrderedEventReplay (reads).
353: 
354: ```mermaid
355: flowchart TD
356:     S(["GzipCodec: operation, bytes"]) --> OP{"Operation?"}
357:     OP -->|Compress| C["Write one GZIP member at the configured level"]
358:     C --> RT[["GzipCodec RoundTrip on the result"]]
359:     RT -->|equal| OK1(["compressed bytes"])
360:     RT -->|different| E1(["evidence_corrupt"])
361:     OP -->|Decompress| D{"Valid GZIP member?"}
362:     D -->|no| E2(["evidence_corrupt"])
363:     D -->|yes| OK2(["original bytes"])
364:     OP -->|RoundTrip| R["Decompress, compare length and SHA-256 with the original"]
365:     R -->|equal| OK3(["equal"])
366:     R -->|different| E3(["evidence_corrupt"])
367: ```
368: 
369: ### 11.3 AuditLedgerGuard (namespace `QBrainAi.Support.Mcp.Storage.Auditing`)
370: 
371: `EnsureAvailable()` checks, inside the caller's transaction, that the `DataAuditLogs` table is writable and refuses with 503 `audit_unavailable` (`retryable: true`) when it is not, closing for HV the skip of `McpDbContext.AppendAuditRows` (`McpDbContext.cs:1507-1538`); `RecordRead(entityKind, entityKey, actor)` adds one ledger row with action `read` for an evidence access (R-19). Every HV unit calls `EnsureAvailable()` before any other step that writes; GetHvEvidenceQuery, GetHvResultQuery, the output stream, and GetHvRequestQuery when it returns output lines call `RecordRead` before returning bytes.
372: 
373: ```mermaid
374: flowchart TD
375:     S(["AuditLedgerGuard: operation"]) --> A{"DataAuditLogs writable in this transaction?"}
376:     A -->|no| E(["503 audit_unavailable, retryable: nothing written"])
377:     A -->|yes| OP{"Operation?"}
378:     OP -->|EnsureAvailable| OK1(["available"])
379:     OP -->|RecordRead| R["Add one ledger row: action read, entity kind and key, actor, request id"]
380:     R --> OK2(["read recorded with the caller's commit"])
381: ```
